author: CodexLiminis
text: The Phong Nhị Massacre — Vietnamese Civilians Killed by South Korea’s Blue Dragon Brigade  On 12 February 1968, South Korean marines came under sniper fire in or near Phong Nhị, central Vietnam. One soldier was wounded.  The Blue Dragon Brigade’s 1st Company, 1st Battalion was operating in the village.  Nguyễn Thị Thanh was a child. Soldiers shot her in the abdomen. Her older brother was badly wounded. Their mother, older sister and younger brother were killed.  She survived multiple operations and about eight months in hospital.  In Phong Nhị and neighbouring Phong Nhất, 74 villagers were killed.  A U.S. report the following month described Phong Nhị as retaliatory killing after Korean troops received fire. It did not establish the full chain of orders. The sniper fire did not prove the civilians were responsible.  U.S. personnel helped the wounded, photographed the aftermath and investigated.  In 2020, Thanh sued South Korea. The government disputed its troops’ responsibility and argued that her claim was too late.  She won in February 2023. An appellate panel upheld the compensation ruling in January 2025.  As a Korean, I could have avoided this subject. But I could not look away.  Speaking for myself, I offer my heartfelt apology to the victims and survivors of these massacres, and their families.  What should acknowledging this massacre require beyond a court judgment?

author: RobLooseCannon
text: Christine Buckley was born in Dublin in 1946. But this baby girl had a Nigerian father which in 1940s Ireland was quite unusual. Christine was placed in Goldenbridge Industrial School in Inchicore, run by the Sisters of Mercy, and there she stayed until her teens.  Goldenbridge was meant to be a place of safety and care for kids. But like most Industrial Schools it was a prison for innocent children where they suffered hunger, beatings and fear. And any difference,  like being a mixed-race child, got you singled out for particular cruelty. Industrial Schools also involved forced child labour. In Goldenbridge girls were made to produce rosary beads in bulk, with punishment waiting for anyone who fell short of the quota. The irony of tarnishing a symbol of love and Gods mother by abusing children forced to manufacture them is a unique evil.  After surviving years of incarceration Christine finally was old enough to leave and trained as a nurse and midwife, and spent years bringing other people's babies safely into the world. Like countless other women failed by the state and church they made a career being kinder and more humane to the innocent.   In 1992, Christine Buckley told her story (and in doing so the story of countless other victims) on The Late Late Show. And sadly, like so many other tales of injustice told before Irish society was able to accept it, the reaction against her was ferocious. She was doubted, attacked and accused of exaggeration. And some of the doubters were powerful and had obvious self interests.   She kept going anyway. The 1996 documentary Dear Daughter put the stories of survivors in front of a national audience, and denial became far harder to sustain. In 1999 the State finally apologised, and the Ryan Report of 2009 confirmed what survivors had said for decades.  Christine Buckley founded the Aislinn Centre to support former residents of the institutions and gave hundreds of them something they had rarely had, a room full of people who believed them. She pressed for redress and for the truth to be told in full.  She was the recipient of the Irish 'Volunteer of the Year' award in 2009. In December 2012, Trinity College awarded her an honorary Doctor of Laws degree in recognition of her work for people who were subjected to institutional abuse. She passed away on 11 March 2014, aged 67, having forced a nation to face its past and also created a better future for girls and women in Ireland.  https://t.co/oTif9EzntZ

author: yulikay
text: I traveled to Asia for the first time, and spent 1 month in Vietnam, Da Nang 🌏🇻🇳  Here's my honest feedback of this trip 👇  People  Probably the first thing I noticed, before traffic or anything else, was how people greet you (except for the airport, because it looked a bit scary at passport control with all the red warning signs lol). Vietnamese people are incredibly nice, kind, and smiling most of the time. It feels like they're just truly happy and want to share that with you.  Food  I don't think there was even one time in a month when we went somewhere and we did not like it. Food is incredible! Perhaps Pho Bo wasn't my favorite, the traditional one, but overall, Da Nang offered great food experiences. Vietnamese, Asian overall, European cuisine, everything tasted really good. I have so many places saved on the map!  Prices  We rented a decent apartment in an expat neighborhood in Da Nang, and it cost around $500/month. You can easily eat on $10 (for 2!). As a woman, I kept up my beauty routine, and I was surprised how affordable it is to look good in Vietnam (nails, laser, beautician, etc.). I even had my first hospital experience there (just for a checkup). It went well and was super cheap compared to Europe.  Traffic and pollution  I cannot forget about these two things, as it was a bit wild for me, especially for the first few days. Even when leaving Vietnam, I was still scared to cross the road as I used to. Pretty much nobody stops, and if you don't learn how to 'go with the flow' and just let bikes/scooters pass you, you're cooked, my friend :)  The air was also pretty polluted most of the time. Once I even didn't feel well because of that and the heat combined (when we wanted to watch fireworks in Da Nang).  Even the fact that the city is by the sea didn't help much. Also, in many areas the city looked really dirty (I just wish the government did something about that, because the nature is beautiful, people are amazing, and it would look so much better if it was clean and neat).  Hoi An, for example, was more peaceful, with less pollution and traffic.  Next time I would rather stay there and go to Da Nang if I really needed to (a taxi from Da Nang to Hoi An was around $11-13, so it's really affordable for such a distance).  Digital nomad experience overall  Vietnam seems like a great place for digital nomads, with a huge variety of coffee places, coworking spaces, and things to do.  Plus, I'm so happy we visited famous Ba Na Hills and the Golden Bridge, the French Village. Yes, we paid $100, which is expensive for Vietnam, but it was a WOW-pass, and it was totally worth it!  If I had to lock in there for some time, that'd be possible even despite some downsides.  Overall, it was a great experience, and I'm happy to be able to explore Asia for the first time.  Now I'm in Chiang Mai, Thailand 🇹🇭, and I'll be happy to share these experiences with you as well!   Let me know if you have any questions in the comments below, and follow my digital nomad journey 🫶

text: gm gm  one month in vietnam today. here are a few things i learned:  -you can eat a proper meal for $1–$2. and i don’t mean snacks. actual food.  -da nang is LOUD. constant traffic, constant beeping, a banh bao guy driving around with a speaker all day, and a garbage truck that plays a melody at 5-6am that woke me up more times than i’d like to admit.  -hoi an surprised me the most. slower, calmer, more nature. i ended up liking it much more than da nang.  -crossing the street is an experience. it honestly feels like cars and bikes here don’t come with brakes. at first it feels impossible. eventually you learn the trick: walk slowly and let the traffic flow around you.  -grab bike rides might be my favorite thing here. for $0.50–$1 someone will drive you 15–20 minutes across the city. -people are kind and many speak basic english, which made things easier than i expected.  these are just a few observations after my first month here. i’m writing a full guide about my experience and tips for vietnam soon.

author: Kenu73
text: Japan Visa 📢  Here's to everyone who is about to apply Japan visa or just want to know about the Japan visa. You are in for a lot of good and legit information.  I have been following the Japan visa since good 2 years now and finally I have almost completed my research to write about it. Let me share what I have learned in years in few lines.   Difficulty level- Easy but occasionally they refuse people randomly, at the same time "easy" isn't like Vietnam or Singapore easy. Don't be overconfident and they do reject visas.   Documents required:-   This can be variable, for example here's the snippet from Delhi, they stick to it unless your overall profile has some discrepancies etc.   They can easily process your visa without any bank statements,  VFS representative removed my bank statements but I insisted to let it be.   There's no job NOC requirement,  dummy tickets are accepted, also as a pro-active step attach 26AS   Cover letter is optional  Plus they are extremely extremely strict about jurisdiction and if you are from Gurgaon, I would still recommend to go to Delhi and apply from there as in Gurgaon they need demand draft for payment and are pretty slow, while in Delhi it's breeze and cash is accepted (no cards)   I gave a photograph, which I had my Schengen visa application done some 2 years ago.   Longer Validity   Now this is something interesting, Japan Embassy randomly hands out 5 years visa and this is where my research was focussed on, many consultants/agents may promise you that we can get you  one and so one but can they? Short answer no. In depth analysis to follow.   My experience   I always get asked by friends family,  how do I travel in such a good budget,  people traveling in India pay more and hence I arranged a group tour for my family and friends where I am taking them to Japan and Korea for 2 weeks, the total cost of the trip came around 70k/person. All flights, stays included, no hostels. Either Airbnb or an Apartment. Visa costs are additional and I am helping all the group members with visa.   I just received my Japanese visa and it took exactly 3 working days.   Vfs was very smooth this time, no appointment needed. Total fees paid 1200 with passport self pick up. I had prepaid and booked everything in advance. I don't do dummy.   Now did I try longer validity ? Yes! I did but still didn't get it.   WARNING ⚠️:- DO NOT PLAN YOUR TRIP FOR MORE THAN 15 DAYS, they as a standard practice issue single entry 15 days and may request multiple/longer but is very discretionary. I know many applicants who lost a lot of money due to this.   Now I have a travel history to all the G7 countries(they focus on this), permanent residenship in one of the G7, my bank statements were top notch, mutliple sources of Income and my job is also well paid with a top MNC, ITR was also solid and I travel a LOT. My passport is full of stamps and infact I could have applied an evisa from home and as a standard got a longer validity but even with this, Japan issued me a single entry 15 days 😅😅   I have now sampled enough to tell you the 5 year visa is absolutely random, as I know a blank passport holder who didn't even give a cover letter get one 😅😅 will update on how it goes for remaining group members.   Meanwhile if you have any questions, feel free to ask in the comments. Yes Japan visa for self employed may pose more documentation and care.   PS- We would now be launching the Japan visa support at viszapp for those who need it.

text: Our SaaS just crossed $13,500 in the last month!  This is how this came to be:  After dropping out one year ago from our CS degree in Spain and having created 3 failed projects in 8 months, my cofounder @PabloSantanaT and I, started working on a new SaaS, RankInPublic.   We tried to ship it as quick as possible, we did it in single 16 hour sprint, from idea to MVP. But then one day I saw two posts, one by @levelsio talking about how if he were broke again he would move to Vietnam and lock in, and another by @tdinh_me talking about how they were building the @HackerResidency in Da Nang (Vietnam).  This seemed like the perfect opportunity. I took my life time savings, $4k, and I booked a one way ticket and a hotel for $190 a month in Da Nang, Vietnam. author: khyatimaloo
text: 🇻🇳There's a Vietnam template that everyone has been following lately. HCMC, Hanoi, Da Nang and Phu Quoc.   And no, I’m not saying skip them. Please go. But also, don’t stop there?!   Here are just a few places in Vietnam worth going to next time you visit:   1. Ha Giang — Dramatic mountain passes, winding roads, and some of the most surreal landscapes in Southeast Asia. Not for comfort seekers. Which is exactly why it’s fun.   2. Ninh Binh — The larger world does it like a day trip from Hanoi. I urge you to stay there for 2 days at least.    3. Phong Nha — Was, is, and will always be my Vietnam. Fell in love with the spot 11 years ago, and have returned back for every visit.   4. Quy Nhon — Underrated coastline, clear waters, away from the tourist traps.  A nice spot if you are seeking that 'live like a local' energy.   5. Da Lat — Cool weather, pine forests, aesthetic cafés just a cosy spot to chill at, away from the big cities.   6. Con Dao — Raw, quiet, and far less commercialised. Slightly eerie if you know its history. Beaches here feel untouched and away from the tourists radar for now.   I’ve done all of these except Con Dao. That’s next on my list unless something else distracts me (very likely).  Which one would you add to your Vietnam Trip?  And if you’ve found a spot that surprised you, I want to know.

text: As a Vietnamese person, I truly feel ashamed and saddened when I witness the actions of some Vietnamese people that are damaging the image of our country in the eyes of Japanese people. But that is precisely why wrongful behavior deserves to be condemned even more, because it can cause other innocent Vietnamese people to face suspicion and prejudice.  I sincerely apologize to the Japanese people who have unfortunately had bad experiences with Vietnamese individuals who have behaved unethically or broken the law. author: sobedominik
text: Left Da Nang and will probably not come back.   Spent a total of 5 weeks here.   I went to bed slightly angry almost every night because of bad service/hospitality, noise, dangerous driving or a mix of those.   It affected my gf even more so we decided to not stay longer than 1 month.  I think that’s a good proxy for liking a place. Our nervous system just never really felt at ease.  In terms of Vietnam in general, I feel like I had a much better time in HCMC when I stayed there for two weeks a few years ago.   Everything seemed to be more efficient there and people were much friendlier.  All my Vietnamese friends are super cool, funny and really friendly.   So I was quite disappointed when I noticed most locals in Da Nang being so cold and borderline unfriendly.  This is the first city in South East Asia this happened to me and if anyone knows why I’d love to learn more about it.   Maybe it was just us? Maybe locals just don’t like tourists/foreigners?   No idea but it felt “off”. Almost not welcomed.  The Indiehacker community is really cool and friendly though.  Some cafes are definitely nice to work from Da Nang and the actual coffee is great. Just strong… very strong hehe  The thing with those coffee shops is just that I’m slowly approaching 30 and can’t sit on ultra uncomfortable chairs for an entire day anymore (👴)  When I first arrived I was super stoked because there are not a lot of nomad spots with breezy sunny weather in Jan/Feb and Da Nang definitely has that.  The cons unfortunately outweigh the pros so I’ll likely not come back for the foreseeable future.   All that being said, if you have a short runway and want to save money it might still be one of the better places to go so I’d say it’s worth giving it a try!

author: andilosing
text: today is my last day in da nang, vietnam 🇻🇳  here are a few things i learned while being here:  – insane good local food + drink for about $2-3  – the city is right at the ocean which gives it a really special vibe  – rent a scooter (~$50/month), there are so many beautiful places to ride to around here and the freedom it gives you is just on another level  – the area around da nang is stunning, some of the most beautiful scenery i've seen  – right now there are a lot of people here from X, perfect place to meet a ton of new and interesting people  – many cozy coffee shops you can work from  – so many people here right now that chances are high you'll run into someone you know at a random café  – the center is super compact, just small streets everywhere and you can walk to basically everything. perfect for coffee shop hopping and grabbing food in between  – you can walk around at any time of day or night and never feel unsafe  – the locals are incredibly friendly. english is often not spoken that well but it's never a problem to communicate (and honestly that's totally fine, i'm in their country so i should be the one learning their language, can't complain if they don't speak english when i don't speak vietnamese)  – if you rent a scooter watch out for the police, they pull you over and ask for a lot of money. don't pay more than $10 (they wanted $200 from me)  – often went on late night walks on the beach which has a really special vibe  – this is the place if you're trying to go all in and not making money yet. you can live here on $600-800 a month (probably the bare minimum budget but still)  da nang is for me the best place i've been so far to try and build a living with my apps: super cheap, right at the ocean, made some great friends here, and so many people with the same goal :)

author: ayusshsanghi
text: No foreign tourist is willing to travel to India.   It is dying slowly.   Let's take an example of Goa.   From 9.37 lakh foreign tourists in 2019 to only 4.67 lakh tourists in 2023.      It has become too expensive for a common traveller to visit Goa.      The opening of other avenues in Southeast Asia, like Vietnam and Indonesia, has also hit Goa's tourism.  You don't have to visit far; you can go to countries like Bali or Vietnam to notice the difference.    Be it:   - Cleaner public spaces.  - Stronger hygiene of street food.  - Stricter plastic control measures.  - Cleaner environment with amazing AQi air.  - Women's safety at night.    No country is perfect, but India is struggling to give very basic things to its citizens.    India can also become like them, even better. India has everything already. History, spirituality, food, art. Colour, Culture and People are amazing here.  Still, we are struggling to attract foreign tourists in India.

text: Planning your first International Trip on a Budget  - Every ₹ matters so choose a country with VOA + No or Less Visa Fee  - The max cost on every trip is the flight and stay cost  - Choose countries which have cheap flights and a good hostel network - Backpacking is not for all I understand but it can save a lot of costs on flights from India and Internal too - Starting with some easy to enter countries helps keep the cost of mistakes also to the minimum. Or a girls only dorm for safety etc. If it clicks, you can stay more days or else move to a hotel.  - Plan your trip but also keep room for changes. While in SE Asia change of plans would not cost much, and you can do it as per your liking. - Travel light. Those Instagram photos with different clothes can wait. Again if the photos bring you joy then please carry bags. Point here has been when you're traveling light you will slowly know what you would prefer, etc, and to make changes will be easier. author: archeohistories
text: Illuminating Hue’s Nhu Y River - a mesmerizing 'Lantern' ceremony, symbolises 'Hope and Peace' in Vietnam :  In the tranquil waters of the Nhu Y River in Hue, Vietnam, a captivating scene unfolds as women, dressed in traditional Vietnamese attire, engage in a ritual of hope and peace. With their iconic conical hats and graceful dresses, these women partake in an age-old tradition, setting about 4,000 flower lanterns adrift on the river. This enchanting ceremony, captured by photographer Nguyen Minh Tuan, is more than just a visual spectacle; it is a deeply symbolic act resonating with cultural significance and communal aspirations.  The lantern ceremony, a poignant and reflective tradition, represents the collective wishes of the local community. Each lantern, delicately placed on the water, carries prayers for health and good fortune. The act of releasing these lanterns is symbolic of letting go of past troubles and embracing a future filled with luck and tranquility. It is also a moment to remember and wish peace for departed relatives, connecting the present with the ancestral past.  As the lanterns, crafted from flowers and candles, gently float down the Nhu Y River, they create a mesmerizing display of light and color. The flickering candles reflect on the water, creating a peaceful and dreamlike atmosphere. This spectacle is not only a feast for the eyes but also a soul-soothing experience, embodying the essence of Vietnamese spiritual life.  The ceremony holds a special place in the cultural fabric of Hue, a city known for its rich history and cultural heritage. Hue, once the imperial capital of Vietnam, is no stranger to traditional rituals and ceremonies. This lantern ceremony is a testament to the city’s enduring cultural traditions and its deep connection with the natural and spiritual worlds.  For locals and visitors alike, the ceremony is an opportunity to partake in a shared cultural experience. It is a moment of collective reflection, an opportunity to pause and appreciate the beauty of simplicity and the power of community. The ritual is a reminder of the enduring human desire for peace, health, and happiness.  The lantern ceremony on the Nhu Y River is more than just a cultural event; it’s a spiritual journey and a celebration of life’s intangible values. It stands as a symbol of the Vietnamese people’s resilience, their reverence for nature, and their deep-seated belief in the power of goodwill and positive intentions. For those who witness it, ceremony is an unforgettable experience, offering a unique insight into the soul of Vietnamese culture and the timeless traditions that continue to shape the heart and spirit of Hue.  © Lynn Hatem 🎥© zayyarlin84 (IG)   #archaeohistories

author: alexcooldev
text: As a Vietnamese person, I think I can add a bit of context to this.  Your experience in Da Nang is actually something I’ve heard from some foreigners before.  HCMC and Da Nang are very different cities.  HCMC has a lot of international companies and expats, so people there are more used to foreigners and English is more common.  It’s also known for having the best service culture in Vietnam.  But the downside is obvious: traffic, noise, and air quality are worse because it’s a fast-growing megacity.  Da Nang is almost the opposite. Pros: - beautiful city - great beach and sunshine - much better air quality - cheaper cost of living  But the trade-offs are:  - smaller city - fewer English speakers - service culture not as strong as HCMC - fewer expat-heavy neighborhoods  In HCMC you have areas like Thao Dien, District 1, District 7 where locals interact with foreigners every day, and many foreigners live and work there long-term.  Da Nang is much smaller, and foreigners are more spread out, so locals may feel more reserved, not necessarily unfriendly.  Ah, one more thing I personally love about HCMC: It’s basically a city that never sleeps.  You can find 24/7 cafes where people are coding, building startups, studying, or working late at night. There are also 24/7 food spots, so you can order something anytime.  That “always moving” energy is something I really enjoy about living in HCMC.  So I’d summarize it like this: HCMC → chaotic but efficient, city that never sleeps Da Nang → beautiful, slower, and more relaxed Both are great cities, just very different vibes.  Maybe in the future service in Da Nang will improve, and if you come back you might have a much better experience. 😁

author: shsunmoon
text: I’ve started to believe much more in designing your environment around the life you want.  My four months in Da Nang made that obvious. I was more productive, less stressed, and generally had more energy to work on things.  A lot of it came down to simple things. Living near the sea. Having sports like pickleball easy to join. Eating healthy food without spending much. Working from good coffee shops surrounded by other people working and building things. Almost never spending more than 15 minutes getting somewhere.  There’s also something about being around people doing similar things. You exchange ideas, learn from each other, and naturally get more motivated. Even things like sauna, cold plunge, yoga, sound healing, or art therapy are accessible enough to become part of normal life instead of something you do once in a while.  I’ve spent time in Seoul, Fukuoka, Frankfurt, Tokyo, Melbourne, Taipei, Hong Kong and other cities over the past couple of years, and you can build a similar lifestyle in many places.  The difference is that in a lot of cities, it gets expensive very quickly. A comfortable short-term apartment, sports, good food, cafés, wellness, and living close to everything can easily add up to a few thousand dollars a month.  That’s what makes Da Nang feel special to me. It’s not that it has something no other city has. It’s that a really good daily life is unusually easy to build there.

author: ErikSolheim
text: What is the world’s most dynamic society in 2026?  It’s Vietnam 🇻🇳!  We are just back from a wonderful family holiday in Vietnam. It is a most amazing place with extraordinary natural beauty, the most friendly people, exciting food, full of life.  Vietnam showed the world that a small developing nation could beat French colonialists and American imperialists. We visited many of the most remarkable sites of the horrible war - the citadel of Hue, Khe Sanh, Ap Bac and Saigon center where the last Americans fled in 1975.  But more striking than anything else is the dynamism of modern Vietnam. No nation today move forward with the same speed. People work hard and smart. The governing system is effective. Vietnam doesnt waste time making enemies. It’s a good friend of the US and China and everyone else.                                                            * Vietnam has achieved a historic drop in poverty, reducing extreme rates from nearly 60% in the early 1990s down to 2-3% today.  * Vietnams economy expanded by 8.2% year-on-year in the first half of 2026, with the government targeting 11.9% growth in the second half to hit a double-digit full-year expansion.  *. Industrial production and manufacturing surged over 10.2% this year, powered heavily by high-tech processing, electronics - working with both China and the US.  * Vietnam is probably the worlds most succesful agricultural nation over the last decades. It was the world’s largest rice importer in the 1980s. It’s now one of the largest rice exporters. Vietnam is the second largest coffee exporter in the wolrd, next to Brazil only. No rocket science - only good policies.  * Vietnam is a miracle of education - it outperforms all nations in the world in tests of 15 years old in school - only exception is East Asian nations like Korea, Singapore and China.  Anyone interested in rapid development - please make a pilgrimage to Vietnam!

author: coinempress
text: five days in da nang and here’s my honest take so far:  first thing i noticed → the airport is ridiculously close to the beach. like 15–20 minutes and you’re at an international airport. for digital nomads or frequent travelers this is honestly heaven.  second → the buildings are kinda adorable. super narrow, tall, almost like stacked apartments. usually just a few units per building. it gives the city a very unique look.  third → baguettes. i knew the history, but i did not expect baguettes to be everywhere and actually good. you order steak? baguette on the side. random meal? baguette appears. not complaining.  food prices surprised me in a good way. if you don’t like cooking and you have a decent income, you can easily eat western food for like $3–7 per meal. pizza, steak, burgers, western breakfast, all super tasty.  the beach is wide and really nice. i get why some people call it the miami of asia. it also feels more modern than i expected.  something i didn’t expect → random karaoke everywhere. small restaurants, tiny bars, street spots. people just sing. dance. vibe. and there are fireworks at night which makes the whole city feel weirdly festive all the time.  crossing the street is a skill you unlock here. zebra crossing means nothing. you just walk slowly and confidently and let the bikes flow around you. survival mode but it works.  one downside → massages are more expensive than thailand and bali. and i lowkey wish there were more coffee shops directly on the beach because working with ocean view is my favorite.  weather right now is also nice. around 25° which feels way easier than 30 in malaysia last week.  overall → da nang feels easy to live in. good food, good prices, modern enough, beach life, fast airport access.  still early review, but so far… i get the hype.

author: khyatimaloo
text: I didn’t start group trips as a business idea. There was no vision board. No five-year plan. They were just...trips I’d take anyway, and thought, why not take a few people along who’d enjoy them as much as I would.  One of the first was an all-women South Korea trip. Somewhere in the middle of planning it, an acquaintance joined in. Not just to join the trip, but to build it together. Same enthusiasm. Same work ethic. Same love for travel. We planned, we executed, and it worked.   Naturally, we assumed this was destiny.  We planned more trips. Announced a few. Watched them not take off. Some were too offbeat. Some were victims of political unrest, or the Indian calendar’s deep attachment to weddings.   Just repeated reminders that the market does not care about your excitement.  Then, Vietnam clicked. Affordable. Familiar. Required just enough leaves to not invite parental concern.   And that’s when my business partner left.  "Group trips don't solve my purpose." She was done. Seven people had already paid.  That sentence did a lot of damage for something so short.  I considered cancelling the trip. Returning the money. Walking away with what little dignity I thought I had left. Not because I couldn’t do it alone, but because I suddenly felt like I’d misunderstood everything. The partnership. The plan. Myself.  I cried to my friends. And they said some annoying things to me:  Who else should take people to Vietnam? You backpacked there in 2015. When Indians didn't know of the region!  Vietnam is literally your home ground. You've been inspiring us to travel before the word influencer marketing was coined!  Annoyingly accurate things. (love you all, you know who you are)   So I went. The trip wasn’t perfect. Nothing ever is. But people laughed. They ate well. They felt safe. They gave feedback. Some of them are coming back for another trip, which still feels surreal.   And then, recently, I saw that the same person who said group trips didn’t serve her purpose is now taking one. To South Korea.  I felt the things you’re supposed to feel. Anger and disappointment. I replayed conversations in my head like a terrible podcast I couldn’t unsubscribe from. I compared. I sulked. I did all the very human things you do when something ends badly.  Then, I felt relief.  Because I didn’t quit when it hurt. I didn’t abandon the thing I loved just because someone else walked away. I didn’t turn joy into ego or scale or a pitch.  I didn’t start group trips to build a legacy or impress strangers on the internet. I started them because travel made sense to me long before growth charts did.  Somewhere in all of this, I found the real point. Not letting the hurt take the wheel.   If you stuck till the end, I hope you find your point too. Also,  thank you for indulging my feelings. It was a long post! :)

author: peeleraja
text: The Vietnam Phu Quoc tragedy brings into focus a little-known fact in India's tourism sector.   Probably the biggest component of outbound international tourism from India is the "dealer incentive package."   Here is how it works. Most brands have dealers. Think mobile phones, cement, servers, bathroom fittings, switch boards etc. How do marketers increase their sales? There are two types of strategies:  1. The "pull" strategy. You design a superior product. You build a killer brand that everyone wants. You price competitively. You make it available easily. You advertise aggressively. These are things that most people recognize immediately as "marketing." You "pull" the customer directly into buying.  Sadly, the pull strategy is not always feasible. Standing out in a commoditized space is not easy. Plus, there may be very strong incumbents whose brand recall you cannot easily match. So you supplement your "pull" strategy with something more insidious - the "push" strategy.  2. The "push" strategy. Say your bathroom tap is leaking. You need to buy a new tap. You immediately think of "Alpha" - you have seen its ads during IPL, its hoardings, etc. You go to the hardware store. He has "Alpha" but tells you to try a new, lesser known "Beta" instead. He sings its virtues and says how it is better than Alpha. Why is he doing it? Because Beta has employed a "push" strategy. They give the dealer a higher margin, better commissions, etc. So he is incentivized to "push" Beta on to you. You do not know if he genuinely loves Beta or is just getting paid to promote it to you.  Sometimes, there are grey areas. Drug companies for example are known to offer push incentives to doctors to prescribe their drugs. The now-defunct Byjus was notorious for offering push incentives to school teachers who got commissions if their students subscribed to it.  Push incentives for things like mobile phones, computers, cement, etc. are not so ethically gray. And a common incentive is of the type, "Sell 1000 units of my product and Thailand Trip free. Sell 2000 and Japan trip free. Sell 3000 and Paris Trip free." This causes retailers, who have otherwise very mundane lives, and often work in crowded, congested market areas, and dirty tier 2 and 3 towns, to put in more effort, to earn that additional freebee - the annual foreign trip.  Naturally these "incentive" trips cost money and eat into the brand's margins. One option is to raise prices, but that is a negative "pull" incentive that will decrease demand. Then the obvious thing to do is to cut costs on the incentive itself, while still delivering that tour package you promised. Offer a Vietnam trip with a boat ride to Phu Quoc, but at the bare minimum price.   You sub-contract to a large outbound travel agency which bulk books hotels, air tickets, and airport transfer in India. But to handle the logistics in a foreign country like Vietnam, they further sub-contract to an inbound travel agency in Vietnam. Who further sub-contracts buses from one operator, boats from another, food from a third, etc. Margins are ultra-thin at the implementation end, with everyone saving money.  Sadly, many of these operators then skimp on essential features. Five extra people in a boat. Ignore if a few life jackets don't have belts. Bare-basics Indian food, because Indian food is expensive in these countries, but the tourists will not eat local cuisine. Plus you often have "that" kind of Indian tourist who is excited about "boys trip to Bangkok" and "hum ab daaru peeyenge."  I learnt a little bit about all of this many years ago from a tour guide who at that point spent 20+ days every month escorting these groups. I suspect one or a mix of all these factors may have led to the tragedy at Phu Quoc. Only a thorough, and hopefully unbiased enquiry will reveal how this tragedy came to be.

author: asksuranaji
text: ✦ The Itinerary ✦   Day 1 – Hanoi Opens Gently  Cyclo Rickshaw Ride → Lotte World Aquarium → Thang Long Water Puppets - the perfect warm-up.  Day 2 – Anniversary on Halong Bay  Comfortable Limousine bus, Breath taking Sung Sot Cave, Ti Top Island, Bamboo boat/kayak in Beautiful Luon Cave lagoons, Veg Indian Meal & cruise rooftop cocktails/hi-tea Dj Party A day that felt tailored for celebration. Booked via Klook ₹3,440 + ₹10k (Times Black Voucher)  Day 3 – Hanoi By Sight & Sound  Double-decker tour → Maison Central (can skip) → Train Street nail-biter timing  → Lotte Observation Deck (reflections from screens behind ruined the pics) → Weekend Night market.  Day 4 – Danang Mornings & Fiery Nights  Linh Ung Pagoda — Monkey Mountain Breeze & Coastal Line View.  Love Pier — Romantic Vibe.  Han & Son Tra — Bustling Market Dragon Bridge Fire Show.  Unreal casual unplanned day spent so well.  Day 5 Ba Na Hills – A Birthday Above the Clouds  A cable car 🚠 ride that felt like a dream. European architecture & cobbled alleys that felt like Hogwarts. Alpine Coaster 🎢 and the thrilling Fantasy Park. A Golden Bridge 🌉  that lived up to its fame And a wife who ended her birthday smiling —  mission accomplished 🙂  Day 6  Quick Recap & Hoi An Evenings  Some experiences call you back, and Ba Na Hills did exactly that. We repeated the Alpine Coaster and Fantasy Park rides in the morning and revisited the Golden Bridge, now wrapped in a mystical fog. The day transitioned into Hoi An with a thrilling basket boat ride, a peaceful walk through the lantern-lit Ancient Town, a serene lantern boat drift, and finally, the spectacular Hoi An Memories Show to close the night.  Day 7 Danang - A Day of Calm & Curiosity  Marble Mountain’s underground caves impressed us, My Khe Beach rested us, and Wonder Park was a chic-click stop for photos. We enjoyed a fun sunset at the resort beach before heading to Vincom Center for shopping. A gentle day of exploration.  Day 8-9 Bangkok in Motion  Asiatique at night was lively and refreshing. The next day, we visited Wat Pho’s reclining Buddha and the Grand Palace glowing golden in the sun. ICONSIAM impressed us with its floating market and indoor waterfall, and we reached the fountain show just in time. Bangkok never disappoints—traffic does—but the city continues to overwhelm in the best ways. We skipped many main attractions this time, as our focus was covering the places we missed on our last trip.  Day 10 Bangkok - The Final Sprint  Platinum Mall, Pratunam Market, Indra Square.  Packing, reflections, and a flight home with bags heavier — minds tired, hearts full...  THREAD 7 of 7 Like - follow - share.  #travelblog #itinerary #vietnam #bangkok

author: 404NOTF65767728
text: The Puppet, The Patron, and The Pariah: Deconstructing the Myth of Nineteenth-Century Cambodian Sovereignty (1594–1840)  Modern ultranationalist revisionism in Phnom Penh routinely manufactures a self-serving historical myth: whitewashing centuries of Siamese tributary suzerainty by asserting that nineteenth-century Cambodia was an autonomous kingdom under Vietnamese dominance, while recasting French colonial gunboat diplomacy as voluntary liberation.  Archival records from Hue, Bangkok, and Paris completely destroy this narrative. Primary documentation—specifically the imperial records of the Nguyen dynasty (Đại Nam Thực Lục), the diplomatic archives of Siam, and the records of the French Ministry of Marine and Colonies preserved in the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)—exposes an unbroken continuum of dynastic instability, strategic duplicity, and deep colonial humiliation.  The Historical Genesis: The Fall of Lovek (1594) and the Cycle of Incurable Vulnerability  The political subservience of the post-Angkorian Cambodian polity did not begin in the nineteenth century; its structural collapse was cemented centuries earlier in the ashes of the Siamese-Cambodian wars of the late sixteenth century. Throughout the Ayutthaya-Burmese wars, the Khmer court repeatedly exploited Siamese vulnerabilities by raiding border settlements and taking captives. In response to this persistent treachery, King Naresuan the Great of Ayutthaya mounted a decisive retaliatory expedition, culminating in the Fall of Lovek in January 1594.  As documented by historian David P. Chandler in A History of Cambodia, the sack of Lovek shattered the psychological and political core of the Khmer state. The royal court was forced into perpetual flight, abandoning one provisional capital after another—relocating to Srei Santhor, Koh Sotin, and eventually settling in Udong in 1618—in a desperate effort to escape Siamese military dominance and the inexorable southward expansion of Vietnam (Nam tiến).  Yet, physical relocation could not compensate for internal decay. Crippled by endemic factionalism and dynastic incompetence, Cambodia’s ruling elite proved utterly incapable of sustaining independent sovereignty. Instead of building national cohesion, rival princes institutionalized a disastrous pattern: invoking the armies of the Court of Hue to seize the throne, realizing in horror that Hue’s ultimate agenda was the total eradication of Khmer culture and territorial absorption, running back to Bangkok on bended knees begging for military salvation, and promptly betraying Siam the moment external danger subsided.  1809–1834: Fratricidal Ambition and the Latin Reality of Dual-Vassalage  The crisis of the nineteenth century was the direct culmination of this incurable cycle. Following the death of King Ang Eng in 1796, his four sons—Ang Chan, Ang Snguon, Ang Em, and Ang Duong—plunged the realm into vicious fratricidal civil war, reducing their kingdom to a geopolitical pawn through a calculated policy of playing Siam and Vietnam against one another.  When the eldest son, King Ang Chan II (r. 1806–1834), ascended the throne under Siamese investiture, he swiftly betrayed Bangkok. In 1809, he refused to attend the royal cremation of King Rama I and actively sought military protection from Emperor Gia Long of Vietnam. In response, his alienated brothers—Ang Snguon, Ang Em, and Ang Duong—fled to Bangkok, begging Siam for troops and arms to overthrow their brother.  This entrenched an infamous strategy of duplicitous dual-vassalage—operating strictly under the Roman maxim of altera manu fert lapidem, panem ostentat altera (offering bread with one hand while holding a stone in the other)—calculated to play both regional empires against each other:  ▪️The Pro-Hue Faction (Ang Chan): Ang Chan invited Vietnamese garrisons into Phnom Penh, allowing Vietnamese mandarins to construct fortresses and dictate foreign policy, simply to protect his precarious throne from his own brothers.  ▪️The Pro-Bangkok Pretenders (Ang Snguon, Ang Em, Ang Duong): The younger brothers weaponized Siamese military backing, staging recurring insurrections that ravaged the Cambodian countryside.  ▪️The Defection of Prince Ang Em (1839): The cynical opportunism of these princes was fully exposed in 1839. Prince Ang Em, whom Bangkok had appointed as governor of Battambang to counter Vietnamese expansion, abruptly defected to Hue. In a desperate bid to win the favor of Emperor Minh Mạng, Ang Em kidnapped thousands of Cambodian civilians and dragged them across the frontier into Vietnamese-controlled territory. Instead of rewarding him with the crown, Minh Mạng arrested Ang Em, stripped him of royal rank, and imprisoned him in Hue—exposing the utter contempt Vietnamese rulers harbored for defecting Khmer royalty.  1834–1840: Hue’s Cultural Eradication and the "Puppet Princess" of Trấn Tây Thành  When King Ang Chan II died in 1834 without a male heir, the Cambodian royal house had completely cannibalized its succession line. Prince Ang Duong was exiled to Bangkok, while Prince Ang Em was imprisoned in Hue. This catastrophic power vacuum allowed Emperor Minh Mạng to execute the absolute dissolution of the Cambodian state.  Hue did not recognize Princess Ang Mey (daughter of Ang Chan II) out of respect for female sovereignty; she was chosen precisely because the squabbling royal factions had eliminated every viable male successor, leaving a powerless woman who could be easily manipulated.  As explicitly documented in the official Nguyen chronicle, Đại Nam Thực Lục (Chính biên, Đệ nhị kỷ), Hue systematically liquidated Khmer statehood:  ▪️Administrative Demotion: In 1835, Emperor Minh Mạng abolished the Khmer crown and formally annexed the realm as the Vietnamese military commandery of Trấn Tây Thành (Western Pacification Command). Princess Ang Mey was formally stripped of sovereign titles and demoted to the bureaucratic rank of Quận chúa (Commandery Princess). She held zero executive power, possessed no royal seal of state, and lived under the constant surveillance of Vietnamese military governors Trương Minh Giảng and Lê Đại Cương.  ▪️Forced Sinicization & Cultural Cleansing: Historian Alexander Woodside (Vietnam and the Chinese Model, Harvard University Press) details Minh Mạng’s forced assimilation decrees. Khmer ministers were compelled to wear Vietnamese tunics and adopt coiled topknots; the Khmer language was banned from official dispatches; and Theravada Buddhist temples were secularized, with monks forced into agricultural labor and military conscription.  ▪️Existential Peril: By 1840, prominent Khmer nobles were being arrested and deported to Saigon and Hue. Left unchecked, the Khmer people faced the exact fate of the Champa Kingdom—total territorial absorption and cultural erasure.  (Continued in Part II: Bangkok’s Armed Salvation, The War of Attrition, and the Rebuilding of a Dynasty)  Archival & Citations:  ▪️Đại Nam Thực Lục (大南寔錄), Chính biên, Đệ nhị kỷ (Minh Mạng court records on the dissolution of Cambodia & Trấn Tây Thành command).  ▪️Woodside, Alexander. Vietnam and the Chinese Model: A Comparative Study of Vietnamese and Chinese Government in the First Half of the Nineteenth Century. Harvard University Press, 1971.  ▪️Chandler, David P. A History of Cambodia. 4th ed. Westview Press, 2008 (Chapters on the Fall of Lovek 1594 & the 19th-century dynastic civil wars).

author: 404NOTF65767728
text: From the perspective of political history and material archaeology, the collapse of the Angkorian center following protracted conflict with Ayutthaya inaugurated the Post-Angkorian era—a period marked by the structural disintegration of classical imperial hegemony. To escape persistent military incursions from Ayutthaya and an expanding Vietnam, the Cambodian court repeatedly relocated its royal seat southward—moving from Angkor to Chaktomuk, Longvek, Oudong, and eventually Phnom Penh. Yet, this geographical flight could not insulate the realm from external domination. Cambodia was inexorably subsumed into the geopolitical crosscurrents of its two powerful neighbors, degenerating into a factional battleground.  The domestic politics of the Cambodian royal family reflected this structural vulnerability: dynastic rivalries consistently led opposing princely factions to solicit external intervention. Whenever one royal faction faced defeat or political marginalization, it sought military shelter and patronage in Huế, offering territorial concessions or vassalage in exchange for Vietnamese backing. Conversely, rival contenders hastened to Bangkok to pledge fealty to the Siamese court, soliciting troops and political investiture to reclaim the throne. As David Chandler observes, this dynamic rendered the Khmer polity a contested domain where "sovereignty was shared, contested, and continually eroded" (Chandler, 2008, p. 139). This cyclical proxy warfare culminated in the protracted Siam-Vietnamese War of 1841–1845 (the Anam-Siam Yuth), a devastating fourteen-year conflict fought on Cambodian soil that concluded with a negotiated condominium: Siam firmly installed and consecrated King Ang Duong upon the throne under Bangkok's paramount administrative tutelage, while Cambodia was simultaneously bound by treaty to remit triennial tribute—most notably the gold and silver flower trees (bunga mas)—to the court of Huế (Woodside, 1971; Chandler, 2008).  During this subsequent era of stability under early Rattanakosin suzerainty, the court at Bangkok exercised decisive hegemony over the reconstruction, institutional patronage, and ceremonial codification of the Cambodian monarchy. This tributary tutelage extended beyond administrative protocol, royal lexicons, and the performing arts (lakhon luang) to dictate elite sartorial norms. Court garments—most notably the drawn hip-wrapper (chong kraben), pleated breast-cloths (pha thaep), and embroidered shoulder mantles (sbai sapak)—were direct adoptions of stylistic standards institutionalized in Bangkok. Documenting this comprehensive courtly transmission, Jean Moura, the French Representative to Cambodia, noted during the reign of King Norodom:  "The costume of the court, the dances, and the court usages differ in no way from those of Siam... the ladies of the palace drape themselves in long silks, following the fashions and manners imported from Bangkok." (Moura, 1883, Vol. 1, p. 415)  Colonial administrator and linguist Étienne Aymonier corroborated this assessment in Le Cambodge, observing that "the high Cambodian society has adopted the costume, the language of the court, and the customs of Siam to such a degree that it is an exact reflection of Bangkok" (Aymonier, 1900, Vol. 1, p. 57). Consequently, the Cambodian monarchy’s eventual capitulation to French protectorate status under the 1863 treaty represented an instrumental diplomatic realignment: an effort to leverage Western imperial power to break free from Siamese suzerainty and forestall Vietnamese demographic absorption.  Accordingly, recent attempts within Cambodian nationalist historiography to trace an unbroken genealogy connecting modern court attire—specifically the pleated and embroidered sbai—directly to the bas-reliefs of Angkor lack empirical grounding in both primary textual sources and the archaeological record. Epigraphic and sculptural evidence from the Angkorian period predominantly portrays deified Hindu-Buddhist personages, ascetics, and celestial figures whose bare-chested presentation conformed to tropical climatic realities and sacred iconographic convention. The fifteenth-century abandonment of Angkor precipitated a multi-century historical rupture characterized by sweeping socio-religious transformations, leaving no intermediate material record to bridge classical epigraphic drapery with modern royal regalia—a cultural discontinuity systematically demonstrated by Bernard-Philippe Groslier (1958).  Deconstructing this anachronistic formulation, Penny Edwards demonstrates how the colonial apparatus actively engineered an "Angkor-centric" paradigm designed to suppress intermediary history:  "In the colonial imagination, and later in Cambodian nationalism, the centuries of Siamese and Vietnamese suzerainty were treated as an aberration or erased altogether, forging an unmediated link between the glories of Angkor and contemporary royal identity." (Edwards, 2007, p. 38)  By excising documented eighteenth- and nineteenth-century Siamese provenance from Cambodian court regalia and retroactively projecting these garments onto classical Khmer antiquity, contemporary revisionist narratives function as exercises in nationalist myth-making rather than evidence-based historical reconstructions.

author: 404NOTF65767728
text: Photography, Historical Timelines, and Distorted Identities: Unveiling the Truth Behind "Queen Ang Mey"  In recent years, Cambodian netizens have frequently circulated vintage photographs of high-ranking noblewomen taken by Western photographers in an effort to assert historical claims. Yet, a fundamental examination of nineteenth-century geopolitics reveals that Bangkok was the undisputed political nucleus and premier international trading port in the region. While early daguerreotype experiments were conducted by European colonial authorities in colonized territories such as the Philippines, Indonesia, and Singapore for exploratory purposes, Siam stands as the first sovereign state in Southeast Asia where the ruling monarch deliberately employed photography as an instrument of statecraft and international diplomacy.  This historic milestone is exemplified by the mid-1850s official portraiture of King Mongkut (Rama IV) and Queen Debsirindra, taken alongside their royal regalia and formally dispatched as state gifts to President Franklin Pierce of the United States and Queen Victoria of the United Kingdom. These archival pieces constitute the very first diplomatic photographs of a sovereign Southeast Asian head of state ever presented to the international community, projecting Siam’s sovereignty, civilization, and preeminence as the suzerain power over neighboring vassal states. In stark contrast, viral side-by-side comparisons across social media and TikTok styling themselves as "Cambodian Queen vs. Vietnamese Empress" reflect a gross misrepresentation spanning political history, photographic science, and fabricated historical identity.  The figure on the left, widely mislabeled across Wikipedia entries and TikTok posts as "Queen Ang Mey" (or Somdet Phra Maha Kasattri An Mei), collapses under both primary-source scrutiny and technological reality. Primary court annals from the Nguyễn dynasty of Vietnam—specifically the Đại Nam thực lục (大南寔錄)—alongside modern historiography by Southeast Asian scholar David Chandler (A History of Cambodia), document that Emperor Minh Mạng systematically annexed Cambodia into the Vietnamese commandery of Trấn Tây Thành (鎭西城) under the absolute rule of General Trương Minh Giảng. In June 1840, Vietnamese authorities stripped Ang Mey of her authority and downgraded her status to Mỹ Lâm quận chúa (美林郡主), equivalent to a mere district-level governor, before subsequently detaining and exiling her to Saigon and Huế. She was never a sovereign "Queen Regnant" in any true constitutional or geopolitical sense, but rather a nominal figurehead tightly controlled by the Vietnamese court.  Crucially, during her nominal tenure (1834–1840), daguerreotype photography had only just been patented in France (1839) and had not yet arrived in Indochina, rendering the physical existence of any photographic portrait of her a scientific impossibility. Official French colonial records at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer (ANOM) authenticate the woman in the photograph as Neak Neang Pen (Samdach Preah Voreak Reachani Pen), the principal consort of King Ang Duong and the royal mother of King Norodom I, captured by French pioneer photographer Émile Gsell between 1866 and 1873. By contrast, the figure on the right depicts Empress Nam Phương of Vietnam on her wedding day in 1934—a chronological disparity exceeding six decades.  The supreme historical irony of this viral meme lies in co-opting Neak Neang Pen’s archival image as "indigenous Cambodian heritage" to compete visually with the Imperial Court of Huế. During the actual reign of Queen Ang Mey, imperial Vietnam implemented sweeping Vietnamization decrees, explicitly outlawing the wrapped chong kraben garment and cropped hairstyles, and mandating that Cambodians grow their hair long and adopt Vietnamese-style áo dài tunics and trousers.  Yet, the archival image of Neak Neang Pen showcases the courtly etiquette of the Early Rattanakosin era in meticulous detail: the pom peek (winged crop) hairstyle, the wrapped chong kraben, the pleated sabai draped diagonally, and courtly regalia on the side table—including traditional pedestaled tiered trays (phan waen fah), footed water basins, and Siamese teapots—all of which represent the court craft of Bangkok’s royal artisans. This cultural continuity was the direct legacy of King Ang Duong, who resided in Bangkok for decades before ascending the throne and systematically revived the royal court of Phnom Penh by adopting Siamese court protocols, master craftsmen, language, and royal attire. Rebranding this image online as "Queen Ang Mey" does not simply forge a revisionist past; it appropriates the visual culture, craftsmanship, and regal heritage of the Siamese Royal Court—the very suzerain power that sheltered and reconstituted the Cambodian court—and projects it as an indigenous identity in direct contradiction to historical reality. (2008). A History of Cambodia (4th ed.). Westview Press: Documentation on Vietnam’s assimilation policies (Vietnamization) during the 1830s–1840s and the restoration of Cambodian court protocols modeled after the Siamese court under King Ang Duong.     ▪️Archives nationales d'outre-mer (ANOM) & Émile Gsell Photographic Collection (c. 1866–1873): French colonial archives authenticating the sitter as Neak Neang Pen, royal mother of King Norodom I.     ▪️National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution (Washington, D.C.): Archival record of the 1856 daguerreotype portrait of King Mongkut (Rama IV) and Queen Debsirindra, presented to U.S. President Franklin Pierce.  #UNESCO #ThaiCulture #StopClaimingThaiCulture #ChudThai #RoyalThaiCostume #IntangibleCulturalHeritage #SaveThaiCulture #Thailand

text: Da Nang Hotels for Couples: Beach, River, or Quiet Resort  Planning a couple’s stay in Da Nang? Compare My Khe beach hotels, a Han River night, and quieter Son Tra resorts before you book.  Da Nang works for couples who want a beach morning and a city night without changing hotels. The right hotels in Da Nang depend on whether the trip is a swim holiday or a slow weekend.  My Khe is the easy romantic base: sand, a pool, and An Thuong dinners a short walk away. The Han River is better if you want the Dragon Bridge on Saturday or Sunday at 9pm and a quieter morning. Son Tra is the pick when you want fewer bars and a more secluded resort.  Book a room that faces the sea or the river, not the coast road. author: saranstm
text: Before Hue became known for the Battle of Hue, one of the fiercest battles of the Vietnam War, it was Vietnam’s imperial capital until 1945. The 1968 battle, fought during the Tet Offensive, left much of the historic city devastated.  Centuries earlier, the region was part of the Linyi Kingdom (2nd–4th century CE), with Kandarpapura as its capital, about 3 km from present-day Hue. Kandarpapura means "the city where Siva burned Kama." Linyi became Indianized through the influence of monks and merchants who brought Indian culture, religious traditions, and ideas to the region.
